model.label: Statutory social health insurance run by a single national fund, with a flat compulsory contribution replacing complementary insurance since 2024

overview.statement: Slovenia runs a statutory, employment-based social health insurance system that offers universal coverage, with the Health Insurance Institute acting as the single purchaser of care.

Mandatory social health insurance was set up in 1992 and runs through one national fund, the Health Insurance Institute of Slovenia, which is funded mainly by payroll-based contributions and covers over 99% of the population.

Primary care is delivered through municipal community health centres with multidisciplinary teams, and GPs act as gatekeepers to specialist and hospital care; some private providers work inside the public system under contracts with the Health Insurance Institute.

Entitlement to the full range of publicly financed care depends on legal residence and on paying the mandatory contributions to the Health Insurance Institute, and people must register in one of 25 entitlement categories.

financing.statement: In 2023 public sources paid 74% of current health spending in Slovenia, against an EU average of 80%; voluntary health insurance (historically complementary cover for co-payments) accounted for 14% and household out-of-pocket payments for 12%, using the OECD health accounts' categories.

WHO's figures for 2023 put voluntary health insurance at 12% of current health spending, the highest share in Europe, and out-of-pocket payments at 13%; WHO's source is its own global health expenditure database.
Public spending on health was 7.1% of GDP in 2023, similar to the EU average but below countries with comparable income per person such as Czechia or Spain.

Social health insurance contributions are the largest source of health revenue; they are set in the 1992 Health Care and Health Insurance Act, are levied on gross income and have stayed unchanged since 2002.
General national and municipal taxation pays for capital investment and national public health programmes such as cancer screening, and finances cover for socially vulnerable groups.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: In 2023 roughly 45% of the population was covered through contributions paid on their own earnings, about 30% through state-paid contributions (for example pensioners, registered unemployed people and social benefit recipients), about 25% as dependants, and under 3% through an annual flat-rate payment.

Since 2024 a fixed compulsory health contribution, set at EUR 37.17 per month in 2025, replaces complementary voluntary insurance premiums; it is charged on all incomes in addition to regular social health insurance contributions, with children and students up to age 26 exempt.

The compulsory health contribution is adjusted yearly in line with the previous year's average salary growth, and the state budget pays the contributions for socially vulnerable and other designated groups.

Parliament adopted amendments to the Health Care and Health Insurance Act on 6 July 2023 that abolished complementary health insurance and replaced it from 1 January 2024 with a fixed compulsory contribution (then EUR 35 a month) collected on all incomes; the Finance Ministry committed to cover potential losses on the scheme up to EUR 240 million.

financing.statement: Before the 2024 abolition, about 73% of residents held complementary voluntary insurance in 2018, and its premiums came to EUR 525.8 million, or 14% of total health spending.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: The 2023 Long-term Care Act sets up compulsory long-term care insurance paid for by employers and employees, who each contribute 1% of salary, with an additional EUR 190 million a year coming from the national budget.

locator.section: 3.2 Sources of revenue and financial flows

financing.statement: Employees paid 6.36% of their gross income towards social health insurance, as reported in the 2021 review.

As reported in the 2021 review, the contribution for illness and injury out of work is 6.56% and a further 0.53% covers work injuries and occupational disease; together with the employee rate, 13.45% of gross income is collected per insured person.

A fixed monthly compulsory health contribution, EUR 37.17 in 2025, took the place of complementary voluntary insurance premiums from 2024. It is raised on every income, sits alongside the regular rate-based social health insurance contributions, and does not apply to children and students up to age 26.

Amendments to the Health Care and Health Insurance Act, adopted on 6 July 2023, ended complementary health insurance. From 1 January 2024 a fixed compulsory payment (initially EUR 35 monthly) is raised on all incomes, and the Ministry of Finance agreed to absorb possible shortfalls of up to EUR 240 million.

covered.statement: The publicly financed benefits package is set out broadly in the 1992 Act, is the same across the country, and includes dental care, orthodontics for children, physiotherapy and long-term care.
Which medicines are covered is decided by the Minister of Health through positive and negative lists, and over-the-counter products are generally not covered.

At the end of 2023 about 0.8% of people eligible for coverage (17,876) were not fully covered because they had not paid mandatory contributions, and 0.3% (5,666) had been in that position for over a year.
By the end of 2024 the number of people not fully covered because of unpaid contributions had fallen to 10,381 (about 0.5% of those eligible), down from 17,876 a year earlier.

Undocumented migrants are not eligible for coverage by the Health Insurance Institute, and adult asylum seekers can obtain most publicly financed care only after approval from the Asylum Centre Commission.

cost_sharing.statement: Between 1993 and 2023 complementary voluntary insurance covered user charges for about 70% of the total population and about 95% of those liable to pay them.
In 2023 pharmaceuticals made up 38% of out-of-pocket payments, outpatient care 26% and dental care 11%.

Most co-payments were abolished in January 2024. The ones that remain are the gap between retail and reference prices for outpatient medicines and medical products, and surcharges for non-standard materials in some dental treatment.
In 2023 the reference-price charge on an outpatient prescription was typically small: under EUR 3 in 59% of cases and under EUR 10 in 97%.

financial_hardship.statement: In WHO's 2022 household-budget analysis, about 1.5% of Slovenian households (around 13,000) had catastrophic health spending, defined as out-of-pocket payments above 40% of capacity to pay, up from below 1% in 2012-2018; the series has a classification break in 2022.
In 2022 about 0.2% of households were impoverished or further impoverished by out-of-pocket payments and about 1% were at risk of impoverishment.

Catastrophic health spending is concentrated among the poorest households: in 2022 just over 3% of the poorest consumption quintile had it, against under 1% of the richest, and the poorest quintile accounted for 43% of affected households.
The biggest contributor to catastrophic health spending in 2022 was dental care (64%); medical products accounted for 15%, outpatient care 11% and outpatient medicines 8%.

additional_care.statement: Supplementary voluntary health insurance remains available to pay for extra specialist care or access to private providers.
Long waits push up take-up of supplementary insurance that offers faster treatment, mainly among higher-income people, which WHO expects to widen inequalities in access.

access.statement: In 2024, 4.6% of Slovenians with a medical need reported unmet care because of cost, waiting time or distance, compared with 3.6% in the EU.
Among people at risk of poverty, unmet medical needs in 2024 were 5.0% in Slovenia against 6.0% in the EU, and unmet dental needs 9.7% against 13.6%.
In 2024 the share of patients waiting more than three months was 90.6% for cataract surgery, 98.6% for hip replacement and 99.3% for knee replacement.

Waiting lists for specialist outpatient care, elective surgery and some diagnostics keep growing despite many government initiatives, which WHO attributes to doctor shortages in some specialities, pandemic disruption and budget pressure.
Slovenia had 3.5 doctors per 1,000 people in 2023, below the EU average of 4.3 and among the lowest in the EU.
About 7% of people with coverage had no registered GP at the end of 2024, a quarter of them migrant workers.

outcomes.statement: Life expectancy at birth reached an all-time high of 82.3 years in 2024, above the EU average.
Mortality from preventable causes was 189 per 100,000 in 2022, down from 212 in 2021 but above the 2019 level of 173.
Thirty-day mortality after heart attack among patients over 45 was 5.7 per 100 in 2023, below the EU average of 6.1.
Mortality after ischaemic stroke has stayed flat and in 2023 was 11.7 per 100 patients, above the EU figure of 9.5.
Avoidable hospital admissions in 2023 were below EU averages for asthma and COPD (103 vs 158 per 100,000), heart failure (205 vs 239) and diabetes (94 vs 116).

costs.statement: Slovenia spent 9.3% of GDP on health in 2023 against 10.0% in the EU, and EUR 3,121 per person (adjusted for purchasing power) against EUR 3,832.
Outpatient care took 33% of current health spending in 2023, well above the EU average of 28%, partly the result of reforms over the past decade that moved patients out of hospitals.

what_works.statement: WHO describes the 2024 abolition of most co-payments as a good-practice example that cut user charges, removed the need for complementary insurance covering co-payments, and lowered system complexity and administrative costs.
Cancer screening rates for breast, cervical and colorectal cancer were 15-20 percentage points above EU averages in 2023: 78% for breast, 74.4% for cervical and 60.8% for colorectal.
Mortality from treatable causes has fallen steadily for almost a decade, much faster than the EU average, reaching 64 per 100,000 in 2022.
In WHO's cross-country comparison of latest available years, Slovenia is among the countries with the lowest incidence of catastrophic health spending in Europe.

problems.statement: WHO warns that heavy reliance on employment-based contributions is a challenge as the population ages, and that unless the revenue base broadens, budget pressure could push up waiting times and erode coverage.
The new flat-rate contribution remains regressive, putting a much heavier burden on lower-income households even though some groups are exempt.
Critical shortages of primary care physicians, outpatient specialists and hospital nurses are partly behind the availability gaps and long waits.
Suicide is a particular problem: 15 deaths per 100,000 in 2022, the fifth leading cause of preventable death, with men nearly four times as likely to die this way as women.

The Observatory flagged that public-sector services fall short of demand and public salaried staff are poorly incentivised, so many work extra or full time for providers serving mostly supplementary-insured patients, which could threaten equity of access.

Because full benefits depend on paying the new flat-rate contribution as well as regular contributions, WHO says there may be a small but significant gap in population coverage, and undocumented migrants are also uncovered.

reforms.statement: Slovenia removed the cap on annual volumes paid to providers in 2022 but reintroduced it in 2023 for most care because removing it had shown no impact on waiting times.

A Renewed Health Service Act limits the circumstances in which public employees can also work for private providers, aiming to strengthen the public system where most professionals are employed, though critics warn that many may leave for the private sector.
Slovenia passed a Healthcare Quality Assurance Act in November 2024, which supported creating the Slovenian Quality Health Care Agency in March 2025.
